title: Sound travels: how a sound gets from where it is made to your ears

summary.text: A grown-up rubs two fingers together. Close by, you hear a soft rustle. Step back a few steps, and the rustle is gone, though the fingers are still rubbing. A sound travels out from its source, through the air, to your ears. It spreads out to every side as it goes, so it gets softer the further it travels. Your child tests how far three sounds can travel in your home, finds that a sound reaches them even from behind and round a corner, and sends their voice one way with a paper cone.
summary.art: A grown-up rubbing her fingers beside her ear at one end of a hallway, and a child standing a few steps away with eyes closed, with small sound lines that fade out before they reach her.

intro.hook: Shut your eyes. A grown-up will tap a spoon on a steel tumbler somewhere in the room. Point to where the sound is. How did the sound find you?
intro.text: You did not touch the tumbler, and you did not see it. Still, the sound reached you. A sound starts at its source, the thing that makes it. Then it travels through the air, all the way to your ears. In this unit you find out how far a sound can travel, which way it goes, and why far-away sounds are soft.
intro.art: A girl sitting on the floor with eyes closed, pointing towards a grown-up, who is tapping a steel tumbler with a spoon across the room.

outcomes: By the end I can say that a sound travels from its source, through the air, to my ears.
By the end I can show that a sound gets softer the further it travels, by testing how far away I can still hear it.
By the end I can show that a sound spreads out to every side, so I can hear it from in front, from behind and round a corner.
By the end I can use a paper cone to send more of my voice one way.
By the end I can say that sound takes a little time to travel, which is why thunder comes after the lightning.

terms.meaning: The sound source is the thing that makes a sound. The sound starts there.
terms.example: When a pressure cooker whistles, the pressure cooker is the sound source.
terms.art: A pressure cooker on a stove with a whistle sound coming out of the top.

terms.meaning: To travel is to go from one place to another. A sound travels from its source to your ears.
terms.example: The cooker's whistle travels from the kitchen to your bedroom.
terms.art: Sound lines going out of a kitchen door, along a hallway, to a girl in her bedroom who looks up.

terms.meaning: To spread out is to go to every side at once. A sound spreads out from its source, like ripples spread out on water.
terms.example: Everyone around a temple bell hears it, in front, behind and on both sides.
terms.art: A brass bell in the middle, with rings of sound lines going out on every side to four children standing around it.

terms.meaning: A megaphone is a cone you speak into. It sends more of your voice one way, so people far away in front of you hear you better.
terms.example: You can make a megaphone by rolling a sheet of newspaper into a cone.
terms.art: A girl speaking into the narrow end of a rolled newspaper cone, with sound lines going out of the wide end.

explanations.concept: A sound travels from its source to your ears
explanations.definition: A sound starts at its source. It travels through the air until it reaches your ears. Then you hear it.
explanations.description: When you tapped the tumbler, it shook very fast. It pushed the air next to it. That air pushed the air next to it, and so on, all the way to your ears. You cannot see this, but you hear the result. A sound can also travel through a wall, so you can hear the neighbour's mixie.
examples: The cooker's whistle travelling from the kitchen to the bedroom
A koel's call travelling from a tree to your window
The neighbour's mixie heard through the wall
Your friend's voice travelling across the room to you
explanations.art: A steel tumbler being tapped on one side of a room, a row of little arrows through the air, and a girl's ear on the other side.

explanations.concept: A sound spreads out, so it gets softer as it travels
explanations.definition: A sound spreads out to every side from its source. The further it travels, the more it has spread out, so less of it reaches each ear. That is why far-away sounds are soft.
explanations.description: In the Walk Away test, the rubbing fingers made the same sound every time. Close by, you heard it well. A few steps back, it was gone. The sound had spread out into the whole room, so only a little of it reached you. A loud sound starts big, so it can spread a long way before it fades. That is why you heard the spoon on the tumbler from much further away than the rubbing fingers. Because a sound spreads to every side, you can hear it from in front, from behind, and even round the corner of a door.
examples: Rubbing fingers heard only from close by
A spoon on a steel tumbler heard across the flat
A temple bell heard by everyone around it, on every side
The cooker heard from round the corner of the kitchen door
explanations.art: A girl in the middle of a room tapping a tumbler, with rings of sound lines spreading out that grow fainter, and three children at different distances: the nearest smiling, the furthest cupping a hand.

explanations.concept: A cone sends more of a sound one way
explanations.definition: A megaphone is a cone that keeps a sound from spreading out to the sides. More of the sound goes out of the wide end, in one direction.
explanations.description: Without a cone, your voice spreads out to every side. Some goes to the walls, some to the ceiling, some behind you. A cone sends more of it forward. So a person in front of you, far away, hears you better. A person behind you hears you less. Many festival loudspeakers are shaped like cones for the same reason.
examples: Cone-shaped loudspeakers on poles at festivals
Cupping your hands round your mouth to call someone
explanations.art: Two pictures: a boy calling with no cone and sound lines going everywhere, and the same boy calling through a paper cone with most sound lines going forward to a friend.

explanations.concept: Sound takes a little time to travel
explanations.definition: A sound does not arrive the moment it is made. It takes a little time to travel. The further away the source, the longer the wait.
explanations.description: In a thunderstorm, lightning and thunder are made at the same moment. The light of the flash reaches you almost at once. The sound of the thunder travels much more slowly. So you see the flash first, and hear the thunder after. Count slowly after you see a flash. A long count means the storm is far away. A short count means the storm is close.
examples: Seeing lightning first, then hearing the thunder
Seeing a cricket bat hit a ball across a big ground, then hearing the knock a moment later
Seeing fireworks burst in the sky, then hearing the bang
explanations.art: A night sky with a lightning flash over the sea, a family at a window counting on their fingers, and a rumble of thunder still on its way.

agreed.text: A sound travels from its source to our ears, through the air or through other things.
agreed.evidence: You can hear a tumbler being tapped without touching it or seeing it. And you can hear a neighbour's mixie through a wall.

agreed.text: A sound gets softer the further it travels from its source.
agreed.evidence: In the Walk Away test, the same finger rub was clear close by and could not be heard a few steps back.

agreed.text: A sound spreads out to every side from its source.
agreed.evidence: In All Around the Tumbler, the sound reached the child from in front, from behind, from the sides and round the door.

agreed.text: Sound takes time to travel, so far-away sounds arrive late.
agreed.evidence: Thunder comes after the lightning. In the 1630s, Marin Mersenne and Pierre Gassendi in France timed the bang of guns fired far away, after seeing the flash.

challenging.claim: Sound only goes forward, the way you are facing.
challenging.who: A common idea among young children
challenging.for: When we talk, we face the person we are talking to.
challenging.against: A sound spreads out to every side. In All Around the Tumbler, the child heard the tap from behind and round a door. A cone can send more of it one way, but without one it goes everywhere.

challenging.claim: A sound arrives the moment it is made.
challenging.who: A common idea, because nearby sounds seem to arrive at once
challenging.for: When someone claps next to you, you hear it straight away.
challenging.against: Sound takes time to travel. Close by, the wait is too short to notice. From far away, you can notice it: thunder comes after the lightning.

challenging.claim: High sounds travel faster than deep sounds.
challenging.who: Greek writers in Aristotle's school, more than 2,000 years ago, and many people after them
challenging.for: High, sharp sounds can seem to reach us quickly and clearly.
challenging.against: In the 1630s, Pierre Gassendi timed the deep boom of a big gun and the sharp crack of a small gun from far away. Both arrived after the same wait.

challenging.claim: A far-away sound is soft because the sound gets tired on the way.
challenging.for: Far-away sounds are softer, and people get tired when they travel far.
challenging.against: The sound spreads out to every side as it travels. So only a little of it reaches each ear far away. A cone stops some of the spreading, and the far sound becomes louder.

big_questions.q: When the finger rub was too far away to hear, was there still a sound in the room?
big_questions.hint: The fingers were still rubbing. Could someone closer still hear it? Could an ant or a cat?

big_questions.q: How does a sound find its way round the corner of a door?
big_questions.hint: The sound spreads out to every side. Some of it goes through the doorway and spreads out again on the other side.

big_questions.q: Why can you hear a cooker whistle in every room, but not a whisper?
big_questions.hint: Think about how big each sound is when it starts, and how much it spreads out on the way.

big_questions.q: When one bell rings, everyone around it hears it at once. Is it one sound, or many sounds, one for each person?
big_questions.hint: There is one bell. But the sound reaches each ear, and each person hears it a little louder or softer.

big_questions.q: If you could follow one sound as it travels, where would it go after it passes you?
big_questions.hint: It keeps spreading: to the walls, out of the window, into the street, getting softer and softer.

story.title: Ammamma's Paper Cone
story.note: Ammamma means grandmother, mother's mother, in Malayalam. Nila, Kannan, Zoya, Amma and Ammamma are made up.
text: Nila was six. She lived on the fifth floor of a tall building in Kochi, with Amma, her little brother Kannan, and her grandmother, Ammamma.
Across the road stood another tall building. On the balcony right opposite lived Nila's best friend, Zoya.
Every evening, Nila and Zoya waved to each other. Then they tried to talk.
"ZOYA!" Nila shouted. "I GOT A NEW BOOK!"
Zoya cupped a hand behind her ear. She shook her head. Down on the road, the autos honked and the buses roared. Nila's words got lost somewhere in the middle.
"She can't hear me," said Nila. "The road is too wide."
Ammamma was folding clothes behind her. "The road is not too wide," she said. "Your voice is going everywhere."
"Everywhere?" said Kannan, who was four. "Where is everywhere?"

"When you shout, your voice goes out on every side," said Ammamma. "Some goes to Zoya. Some goes up to the sky. Some goes down to the autos. Some goes back into our flat. So only a little bit gets to Zoya."
Ammamma picked up an old newspaper. She rolled it into a long cone, wide at one end and narrow at the other. She stuck it with a strip of tape.
"When I was a girl, our house stood at the edge of the paddy fields," she said. "My mother used a cone like this to call us home for lunch. Every child in the fields heard her."
Nila put the narrow end to her mouth. She pointed the wide end at Zoya's balcony.
"Zoya!" she called. She did not shout this time. She only used her ordinary calling voice. "I got a new book!"
Across the road, Zoya jumped. She gave a big thumbs up. Then she ran inside.
A minute later, Zoya came back with her own rolled-up newspaper. "What book?" she called through it.
Nila could hear her, even over the honking. She laughed. "A book about the sea!"
Kannan pulled Ammamma's sari. "Why does the cone work?"
"Without the cone, your voice spreads out on every side," said Ammamma. "The cone keeps it from going to the sides. So more of it goes straight to Zoya."
Kannan took the cone. He turned round and pointed it at Amma in the kitchen. "Amma, I'm hungry!" he called.
"I can hear you, Kannan," said Amma, laughing. "Dinner is coming."
That night it rained, the way it rains in Kochi in June. The whole sky went white for a moment.
"Lightning!" said Nila.
"Now count with me, slowly," said Ammamma. "One. Two. Three. Four. Five. Six."
BOOM. The thunder rolled over the buildings.
"Why did the thunder come so late?" asked Nila. "Did it get lost?"

"The lightning and the thunder were made at the same moment, far away over the sea," said Ammamma. "The light reached us almost at once. The sound had to travel all the way here. Sound takes a little time to travel."
There was another flash. They counted together. One. Two. Three. BOOM.
"Only three this time," said Nila. "So the storm is coming closer."
"Yes," said Ammamma. "A short count means a close storm."
Kannan pulled his blanket up to his nose. "Will it come all the way here?"
They counted the next flash. One. Two. Three. Four. Five. Six. Seven. BOOM, much softer.
"Seven!" said Nila. "It's going away again."
"And the thunder is softer," said Kannan. "Because it spread out on the way?"
Ammamma smiled. "You have both learned something today. A sound starts in one place. Then it travels, and it spreads out on every side as it goes."
Nila looked out at the dark balcony across the road. Zoya's light was still on. Nila picked up the paper cone and whispered into it. "Good night, Zoya."
It was only a whisper. But across the road, the light blinked off and on again.
story.epiphany: A sound starts at its source and spreads out on every side as it travels. A cone sends more of it one way, so a friend far away hears it better. Sound also takes time to travel, so thunder comes after the lightning, and a longer wait means the storm is further away.
ask: Why couldn't Zoya hear Nila's shout across the road?
How did Ammamma's paper cone help Zoya hear Nila?
Why did the thunder come after the lightning?
When the count got longer, what did Nila know about the storm?
art: Two tall buildings across a busy road in Kochi, and two girls waving from balconies opposite each other, with autos and buses below.
A grandmother in a sari rolling an old newspaper into a long cone on a balcony, a girl and a small boy watching.
The girl calling through the paper cone towards her friend across the road, and her friend giving a thumbs up.
A family at a window at night in the rain, a white flash of lightning over the sea, the girl counting on her fingers.
The girl whispering good night into the cone, and a light blinking in a window across the road.

experiments.title: Walk Away: how far can you hear it?
experiments.context: In this experiment a grown-up makes three different sounds. You walk away, one step at a time, until you cannot hear each one any more. You mark the spot for each sound and see which one travels furthest.
experiments.question: Does every sound travel the same distance before you stop hearing it? And does a hard crinkle travel further than a gentle one?
experiments.predict: The grown-up will rub fingers, crinkle a plastic bag and tap a spoon on a steel tumbler. Which sound will you hear from furthest away? Which will fade first? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The grown-up stays on the same spot and holds each sound at the same height, next to their shoulder. They make each sound the same way each time. You take the same small steps, one heel touching the other toe, and you close your eyes before each sound.
results_table: My guess: near, middle or far?
Steps until I could not hear it

materials.item: a long hallway, or a room with the door open to the next room: the longest straight line in your home
a plastic carry bag or a sheet of crinkly paper
a steel tumbler and a steel spoon
3 chappals, or 3 pieces of coloured paper, to mark the spots
a sheet of paper and a pencil for the results

schedule.what: Guess which sound travels furthest, walk away from each sound until it fades, and mark the spots.

experiments.record: Draw the hallway as a long box. Draw the grown-up at one end. Draw a chappal for each sound where it faded, with a small picture of the sound next to it: fingers, a bag, a tumbler.

setup.art: A grown-up standing at one end of a hallway in a flat, holding a steel tumbler, a spoon and a plastic bag, and a child standing next to her.
setup.caption: 1. The grown-up stands at one end. You start right next to them.

setup.art: The girl with her eyes closed, a few steps away, while the grown-up rubs two fingers together beside her own ear.
setup.caption: 2. Close your eyes. Say yes if you hear the sound.

setup.art: The girl taking one small heel-to-toe step backwards along the hallway.
setup.caption: 3. Each time you hear it, take one more step back.

setup.art: The hallway floor with three chappals at different distances from the grown-up, the nearest beside a picture of fingers and the furthest beside a tumbler.
setup.caption: 4. Put a chappal where each sound faded. Which went furthest?

flow.do: 1. Switch off the fan, the TV and any music. 2. Find the longest straight line in your home. 3. Stand at one end with the bag, the tumbler and the spoon.
flow.say: We are going to find out how far a sound can travel in our home. First, let's make the house quiet.
flow.kid: Help make the house quiet. Switch off the TV and the fan.
flow.parent: A hallway, or two rooms joined by an open door, works well. Other noises make sounds fade sooner, so a quiet time of day helps.

flow.do: Make each sound once while your child stands next to you. Rub your thumb and finger together beside your ear. Crinkle the bag. Tap the tumbler gently with the spoon.
flow.say: Here are our three sounds. Listen to each one. Which will you hear from furthest away? Which will fade first? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Listen to the three sounds. Which will you hear from far away? Why?

ask.q: Which sound do you think will go furthest? Why?
good: The tumbler, because it is loudest.
The bag, because it is crinkly.
The fingers, because I can hear them well now.

flow.parent: Write the guesses in the table. Any guess with a reason is good. Don't say what will happen.

flow.do: 1. Your child closes their eyes. 2. Rub your fingers beside your ear, three times. 3. If they say yes, they take one heel-to-toe step back. 4. Repeat until they say no twice. 5. Put a chappal on that spot.
flow.say: Close your eyes. Say yes if you hear it. Then take one step back. Say no if you can't hear it.
flow.kid: Close your eyes. Can you hear it? Say yes, then step back.

ask.q: How many steps did you take before the finger rub faded?
good: Only a few steps.
Four steps, then I could not hear it.

flow.parent: Keep your fingers at the same height each time, and rub the same way. The finger rub usually fades after a few small steps. Sometimes say 'now', and make no sound. This checks that your child is listening, not guessing.

flow.do: 1. Your child comes back to your side. 2. Do the same with the bag, crinkled gently. 3. Then with the spoon tapped gently on the tumbler. 4. Put a chappal where each sound faded.
flow.say: Now the bag, crinkled gently. Same rules. Close your eyes, say yes, and step back. Now the tumbler.
flow.kid: Now the bag. Then the tumbler. Step back each time you hear it.

ask.q: Which sound did you hear from furthest away?
good: The tumbler.
The spoon on the steel.

flow.parent: If your child reaches the wall and can still hear the sound, put the chappal at the wall. That sound travels further than your home is long. The tumbler often goes the whole way.

flow.do: 1. Stand your child at the chappal for the bag. 2. Crinkle the bag gently, then hard. 3. Ask which one they heard.
flow.say: You are standing where the bag faded. I will crinkle it gently. Now hard. Which one could you hear?
flow.kid: Listen. A gentle crinkle. Now a hard one. Which can you hear?

good: The hard one.
I heard the hard one, not the gentle one.

check.q: Which sound can travel further before it fades?
options: They both fade at the same spot
check.why: A hard crinkle makes a bigger sound to start with. It can spread out a long way and still be loud enough to hear. A gentle crinkle is small from the start, so it fades sooner.

flow.do: 1. Look at the three chappals together. 2. Count the steps to each one. 3. Ask your child to tell you three things, and write them in their words.
flow.say: Look at our chappals. Which sound went furthest? Tell me what you think now, what you heard, and why you think it happened.
flow.kid: Look at the chappals. Which sound went furthest? Why?
flow.parent: A strong answer sounds like this. 'The fingers faded first and the tumbler went furthest. Far away, the sounds got softer. A big sound can travel further before it fades.' Later you can add: the sound spreads out to every side, so less of it reaches you far away.

experiments.title: The Paper Cone: can we send a sound one way?
experiments.context: In this experiment you roll a newspaper into a cone. A grown-up says the same words with and without the cone, and with the cone pointing at you or away from you. You listen from far away.
experiments.question: Does a paper cone make a voice easier to hear from far away? Does it matter which way the cone points?
experiments.predict: The grown-up will say the same words three ways: with no cone, with the cone pointing at you, and with the cone pointing at the wall. Which way will be clearest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The grown-up stays on the same spot and uses the same quiet voice each time. You stay at the same far spot. The words are different each time, so you cannot guess them.
results_table: My guess: clear, a little, or not at all?
What I heard: clear, a little, or not at all?

materials.item: a hallway or two rooms with an open door

schedule.what: Make a paper cone, then listen from far away to a voice with and without it.

experiments.record: Draw the grown-up speaking three ways: no cone, cone pointing at you, cone pointing at the wall. Draw a smiling ear next to the clearest one.

setup.art: A grown-up and a boy rolling two sheets of newspaper into a long cone, wide at one end, and sticking it with tape.
setup.caption: 1. Roll the newspaper into a cone and tape it.

setup.art: The boy standing at the far end of a hallway, and the grown-up at the other end speaking quietly with no cone.
setup.caption: 2. Go far away. Listen to the voice with no cone.

setup.art: The grown-up speaking into the narrow end of the cone, with the wide end pointing straight at the boy.
setup.caption: 3. Listen again, with the cone pointing at you.

setup.art: The grown-up speaking into the cone pointing at the side wall, and the boy leaning forward to listen.
setup.caption: 4. Listen once more, with the cone pointing at the wall.

flow.do: Lay two sheets of newspaper on top of each other. Roll them into a cone, wide at one end and narrow at the other. Tape it.
flow.say: We are making a megaphone. A megaphone is a cone you speak into. Let's see what it does.
flow.kid: Roll the newspaper into a cone. Make one end wide. Tape it.
flow.parent: Make the narrow end about as wide as your mouth, and the wide end about as wide as a plate. A cone about as long as your arm works well.

flow.do: 1. Your child stands far away, at the spot where a quiet voice is only just clear. 2. Ask them to guess which way will be clearest, and why.
flow.say: I will say some words three ways: no cone, cone at you, and cone at the wall. Which will be clearest? Why?
flow.kid: Which way will you hear best? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Which way do you think will be clearest?
good: The cone pointing at me.
The cone, because it is like a loudspeaker.

flow.parent: Find the spot by talking quietly and asking your child to step back until your words are only just clear. A whisper works too.

flow.do: 1. Say a short sentence quietly with no cone. 2. Say a new sentence the same way through the cone, pointing at your child. 3. Say a third sentence with the cone pointing at the side wall. 4. Each time, your child says what they heard.
flow.say: Listen. Tell me the words you heard. Was it clear, a little, or not at all?
flow.kid: Listen. Say the words you heard. Was it clear?

good: When the cone pointed at me.
With the cone, facing me.

flow.parent: Keep your voice at exactly the same loudness. Use new words each time, like 'Idli for breakfast', 'The crow is on the wall', 'Ten red bangles'. Usually the cone pointing at your child is clearest, and the cone pointing at the wall is the hardest to hear. The change is small but real. If you cannot tell the difference, stand a few steps further back.

flow.do: Ask your child to tell you three things. Write them down in their words.
flow.say: What do you think now? What did you hear? Why do you think the cone helped?
flow.kid: Say what you think. Say what you heard. Say why.

check.q: Your friend is far away, in front of you. Which way should the wide end of the cone point?
check.why: The cone keeps your voice from spreading to the sides, and sends more of it out of the wide end. So point the wide end at the person you want to hear you.

flow.parent: A strong answer sounds like this. 'With the cone pointing at me, the words were clearest. Pointing at the wall, they were hard to hear. The cone sends the voice one way, instead of to every side.'

activities.title: All Around the Tumbler
activities.context: In this activity a grown-up taps a steel tumbler in the middle of a room. You stand in front, behind, at the sides and round the door, and listen. Does the sound reach every spot?

materials.item: a steel tumbler and a spoon

schedule.what: Listen to a tapped tumbler from in front, behind, the sides and round the door.

activities.record: Draw the tumbler in the middle of the page. Draw yourself in every spot where you heard it. Draw sound lines going out from the tumbler to every side.

setup.art: A grown-up sitting on a stool in the middle of a room, tapping a steel tumbler with a spoon, and a girl standing in front of her with eyes closed.
setup.caption: 1. Stand in front. Close your eyes. Listen to the tap.

setup.art: The same room seen from above, with footprints showing the girl standing in front, behind, at both sides and just outside the door.
setup.caption: 2. Stand behind, at the sides and round the door. Listen each time.

flow.do: Sit in the middle of the room with the tumbler. Your child stands in front of you, about three steps away. Tap the tumbler gently twice.
flow.say: Close your eyes. I will tap the tumbler. Point to where the sound is.
flow.kid: Close your eyes. Listen. Point to the sound.

ask.q: How did the sound get to you?
good: It came through the air.
It came from the tumbler to my ears.

flow.do: Ask your child to stand behind you, then at your left, then at your right. Last, they stand just outside the door, round the corner, where they cannot see you. Tap the same way each time.
flow.say: Now stand behind me. Can you hear it? Now at the side. Now go round the door, where you can't see me. Can you still hear it?
flow.kid: Stand behind. Now at the side. Now round the door. Can you hear it?

ask.q: Where could you hear the tap?
good: Everywhere.
Even behind and round the door.

flow.parent: Your child will hear the tap in every spot, even round the door. It may sound a little softer there. Don't explain yet. Let them notice.

flow.do: Ask your child what they found. Then ask them to draw it.
flow.say: The tumbler is in one place. But you heard it in front, behind, at the sides and round the door. What does that tell you about the sound?
flow.kid: You heard it everywhere. Which way did the sound go?

ask.q: Which way does a sound go from the tumbler?
good: Every way.
It spreads out to all sides.

flow.parent: The word to bring in now is 'spread out'. The sound spreads out to every side from its source, like ripples on water.

activities.title: Count After the Lightning
activities.context: In this activity you watch a thunderstorm from a window. After each flash of lightning, you count slowly until you hear the thunder. A long count means the storm is far away.

materials.item: a window or a covered balcony, on a stormy evening
a sheet of paper and a pencil

activities.safety: Watch from inside, through a window or from a covered balcony. Stay away from open terraces, water and tall trees in a storm.

schedule.what: On a stormy evening, count from each lightning flash to its thunder.

activities.record: Draw a line of lightning flashes. Under each one, write or draw the count you got: for example, five dots for a count of five.

setup.art: A boy and his mother at a closed window at night, a white lightning flash far away over the city.
setup.caption: 1. Watch for a flash of lightning.

setup.art: The boy holding up fingers as he counts, and his mother writing the number on a paper.
setup.caption: 2. Count slowly until you hear the thunder.

flow.do: On a stormy evening, sit with your child by a closed window or on a covered balcony.
flow.say: Watch the sky. When you see a flash, we will count slowly together until the thunder comes.
flow.kid: Watch the sky with a grown-up. Wait for a flash.
flow.parent: This activity needs a storm, so do it when one comes. During the monsoon that is often. If there is no storm this week, keep it for later.

flow.do: After each flash, count slowly together: one, two, three. Stop when the thunder comes. Write the number. Do this for three or four flashes.
flow.say: Flash! One. Two. Three. Four. There's the thunder. What number did we get?
flow.kid: Flash! Count slowly. Stop at the thunder. What number?

ask.q: Why does the thunder come after the flash?
good: The sound takes time to come.
The thunder has to travel to us.

flow.do: Look at the numbers together.
flow.say: Look at our numbers. Are they getting bigger or smaller? Is the storm coming closer, or going away? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Are the numbers getting bigger or smaller? What does that mean?

ask.q: What does a bigger count mean?
good: The storm is further away.
The sound had further to travel.

flow.parent: Lightning and thunder are made at the same moment. The light arrives almost at once. The sound takes about three seconds to travel one kilometre. So a longer count means a storm further away.

activities.title: Be the Air: pass the sound along
activities.context: In this act-out, the family stands in a line from a drum to an ear. Each person passes a gentle tap to the next, the way the air passes a sound along, until it reaches the ear at the end.

materials.item: 2 or more people, and a steel plate or a box to be the drum
a sheet of paper and tape, for the paper ear

schedule.what: Stand in a line and pass a tap from the drum to the ear, the way air passes a sound along.

activities.record: Draw your family in a line, with a drum at one end and a big ear at the other. Draw arrows from each person to the next.

setup.art: A girl at one end of a line of three family members, tapping a steel plate, and a big paper ear taped to the wall at the other end.
setup.caption: 1. One person is the drum. The others are the air.

setup.art: Each family member gently tapping the shoulder of the next person in the line, and the last one touching the paper ear.
setup.caption: 2. Pass the tap along, one shoulder to the next, to the ear.

flow.do: Draw a big ear on a paper and tape it to a wall. Everyone else stands in a line between the steel plate and the ear, facing the ear.
flow.say: The plate is the sound source. The paper is an ear. We are the air in between.
flow.kid: The plate makes the sound. The paper is an ear. We are the air.
flow.parent: With only two people, you tap the plate and your child is the air. They pass the tap on to the paper ear.

flow.do: The first person taps the plate once, then gently taps the shoulder of the next person. Each person passes the tap on. The last person touches the ear and says 'I hear it!'
flow.say: Tap the plate, then tap the next shoulder. Pass it on. When it reaches the ear, say 'I hear it!'
flow.kid: Feel the tap on your shoulder. Pass it on gently.

ask.q: Did anyone walk to the ear?
good: No.
We stayed in our places. Only the tap moved.

flow.do: Talk about what happened.
flow.say: Nobody walked to the ear. But the tap got there. How is that like a sound going through the air?
flow.kid: Nobody walked. But the tap reached the ear. How?

ask.q: How does a sound get from the plate to your ear?
good: The air passes it along.
The air next to the plate pushes the next air, all the way to my ear.

flow.parent: This is a model, a way of showing what we cannot see. The air does not rush from the plate to your ear. Each bit of air pushes the next bit, and the push travels.

games.title: Whisper Walk
games.players: 2 or more: a whisperer and one or more walkers. A grown-up whispers first.
games.context: This is a listening game. The whisperer stands at one end and whispers a word from a card. The walkers start far away and come one step closer each time, until someone can hear the word.

img.credit: Morten Ross, CC BY, via iNaturalist
Parth Kansara, CC BY, via iNaturalist

rules: Cut out the cards and put them face down.
The whisperer stands at one end of the room or the hallway.
The walkers stand at the far end, next to each other.
The whisperer picks a card and whispers the word. A child who cannot read yet gets the word whispered to them by a grown-up first.
If no walker can hear it, every walker takes one step closer, and the whisperer whispers the same word again.
The first walker to say the word right keeps the card.
Everyone goes back to the far end for the next card, and the next person becomes the whisperer. When the 6 cards run out, the most cards wins. If the cards are level, everyone wins.

setup.art: A grown-up whispering at one end of a hallway, holding a word card, and two children standing at the far end, listening.
setup.caption: 1. The whisperer whispers a word. The walkers listen from far away.

setup.art: The two children one step closer, one of them putting up her hand to say the word.
setup.caption: 2. Can't hear it? Step closer. First to say the word keeps the card.

flow.do: Cut out the cards. Read the rules together. You whisper first.
flow.say: I will whisper a word from far away. If you can't hear it, take one step closer. Let's see how close you need to come.
flow.kid: Listen for the whisper. Can't hear it? Take one step closer.
flow.parent: Many children of 6 cannot read the cards yet. You read each card, then whisper the word to them to pass on.

flow.do: Play three cards. Whisper at the same softness each time. After each card, count how many steps the walkers took.
flow.say: Here is a word. Can you hear it? No? Take a step. Now?
flow.kid: Can you hear the word? Say it! Or take a step.

ask.q: Why did you have to come closer?
good: The whisper was too soft from far away.
Close up, more of the whisper reaches me.

flow.parent: Keep the whisper equally soft each time, so the game is fair.

flow.do: Play the last three cards. The next person whispers each time, so your child whispers too.
flow.say: Now you whisper, and I walk. Do you think I will need more steps or fewer than you?
flow.kid: Now you whisper. Make it soft!

check.q: The walkers could not hear the whisper. What made it easier to hear?
check.why: A sound spreads out as it travels, so it gets softer far away. Close to the whisperer, more of the whisper reaches your ears.

flow.parent: Read the card to your child quietly, so they can whisper the word to you.

games.title: Who Hears It Louder? A card game
games.players: 1 to 4 players. A grown-up reads the cards and does not play.
games.context: This is a card game about sounds travelling. A grown-up reads a card. The players answer and act out the sound if they can.

items.f: A temple bell rings. Meena stands next to the bell. Her friend is at the end of the street. Who hears it louder?
items.b: Meena. She is close, so more of the sound reaches her.

items.f: The cooker whistles in the kitchen. Arjun is in the bedroom. Can he hear it?
items.b: Yes. The whistle travels through the air, out of the kitchen door, to the bedroom.

items.f: Kavya's grandmother claps behind Kavya's back. Can Kavya hear the clap?
items.b: Yes. A sound spreads out to every side, so it reaches you from behind too.

items.f: A storm is far away. You see a flash of lightning. What comes next?
items.b: The thunder, a little later. The sound takes time to travel to you.

items.f: Lakshmi whispers to Farhan from across a big room. He can't hear. What can he do?
items.b: Come closer. A whisper fades as it travels, so it is easier to hear close by.

items.f: Riya calls through a paper cone. Should the wide end point at her friend, or at the floor?
items.b: At her friend. The cone sends more of the sound out of the wide end.

items.f: A koel calls from a tree far away, and another koel calls just outside the window. Both calls are equally loud to start with. Which call sounds louder to you?
items.b: The call outside the window. That sound has travelled less far.

items.f: A boy rides his cycle down the lane towards your door, ringing his bell. Does the bell get louder or softer as he comes closer?
items.b: Louder. Each step he comes closer, the sound has less far to travel.

items.f: The neighbour's mixie is running behind the wall. Can you hear it?
items.b: Yes. Sound can travel through walls, as well as through air.

items.f: Ammu stands round the corner of a door. Amma rings a bell in the room. Can Ammu hear it?
items.b: Yes, a little softer. The sound spreads out through the doorway and round the corner.

rules: Shuffle the cards and put them face down.
A grown-up reads the top card out loud. The players take turns to answer.
The player whose turn it is answers, and gives a reason. Then they act it out if they can: ring, clap, whisper or whistle.
The grown-up turns the card and reads the answer. A good answer with a reason keeps the card. If not, the card is put aside.

The game ends when all 10 cards have been read. The most cards wins. If the cards are level, everyone wins. With one player, keep as many of the 10 cards as you can, then play again and try to beat your score.

setup.art: Two children and a grown-up sitting on a mat with a pile of cards, the grown-up reading one out.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up reads a card. Who hears it? Near or far?

setup.art: One child standing far away and one close to a clapping grown-up, acting out a card.
setup.caption: 2. Act it out, then turn the card to check.

flow.do: Cut out the cards. Read the rules together.
flow.say: I will read a card. You tell me who hears the sound, or what happens. Then we try it.
flow.kid: Listen to the card. Who hears it? Then try it.

flow.do: Read the cards one by one. After each answer, ask why. Act out the ones you can at home.
flow.say: Who hears it louder? Why do you think so? Let's try it.
flow.kid: Who hears it louder? Why? Let's try!

ask.q: Why does the person far away hear it more softly?
good: The sound spreads out on the way.
Less of it reaches them.

flow.do: Count the cards each player kept.
flow.say: Which card was the trickiest? Why?
flow.kid: Count your cards. Which was the hardest?

projects.title: Where Can You Hear the Cooker?
projects.context: In this project you draw a map of your home. Then, when the pressure cooker whistles, you go from room to room and mark how loud the whistle is in each one.

materials.item: a big sheet of paper and crayons in 3 colours: red, yellow and blue
a pressure cooker being used for cooking, by a grown-up

projects.safety: Only a grown-up uses the pressure cooker. Your child listens from the kitchen door and never goes near the stove.

schedule.what: Draw a simple map of your home, with a box for each room.
When the cooker whistles, listen in each room and colour it: red for loud, yellow for soft, blue for can't hear.

projects.record: The finished map, with the kitchen and the cooker marked, and each room coloured red, yellow or blue.

setup.art: A child's map of a flat with boxes for the kitchen, the hall, two bedrooms, a bathroom and a balcony, and a cooker drawn in the kitchen.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a box for each room. Draw the cooker in the kitchen.

setup.art: A girl standing in a bedroom doorway listening, with the cooker whistling far away in the kitchen.
setup.caption: 2. When the cooker whistles, stand in each room and listen.

setup.art: The same map coloured in: the kitchen and hall red, the bedrooms yellow, and the far balcony blue.
setup.caption: 3. Colour each room: red for loud, yellow for soft, blue for can't hear.

flow.do: Walk round your home with your child. On the paper, draw a box for each room, in roughly the right places. Draw the cooker in the kitchen.
flow.say: Let's draw our home. Here is the kitchen. What room is next to it? Where is your bedroom?
flow.kid: Draw a box for each room. Draw the cooker in the kitchen.
flow.parent: The map does not need to be neat. A box for each room, joined where the doors are, is enough.

flow.wait: Do this the next time you cook with the pressure cooker.
flow.do: When the cooker starts to whistle, your child goes to each room and listens. They tell you loud, soft or can't hear. Colour each room on the map.
flow.say: The cooker is whistling. Go to the bedroom. Is it loud, soft, or can't you hear it? Now the balcony.
flow.kid: The cooker is whistling! Go to each room. Loud, soft, or can't hear?

ask.q: Where was the whistle loudest? Where was it softest?
good: Loudest in the kitchen.
Softest in the far bedroom with the door shut.

flow.parent: A cooker whistles several times, so there is time to visit each room. In a small flat the whistle may be heard everywhere. Then use only red and yellow. Stay with your child near the kitchen.

flow.do: Look at the finished map together.
flow.say: Look at the colours. Where is the red? Where is the blue? Why do you think the whistle was soft in some rooms?
flow.kid: Look at the colours. Why was it soft in some rooms?

ask.q: Why was the whistle soft in the far rooms?
good: It had further to travel.
It spread out on the way.
The door was shut.

flow.parent: Rooms far from the kitchen are softer, because the sound has spread out more. A shut door also makes the sound softer.

challenges.title: The Far Room Doorbell
challenges.context: This is a problem to solve. Someone sits in the far bedroom with the door half shut and often misses the doorbell. How can you help the sound reach them?
challenges.problem: Someone likes to sit in the far bedroom, with the door half shut. When the doorbell rings, they do not hear it. How can you help the sound of the bell, or of a visitor's knock, travel to the far room?
constraints: The listener stays in the far room.
Use only things you already have at home.
The neighbours should not be disturbed.
materials: a steel tumbler and a spoon, to be the doorbell
a phone that can play a ringing sound, if you have one
general: Open the bedroom door, so the sound does not have to go round a corner.
Open the doors between the front door and the far room.
creative: Put a second bell, or the phone, half-way between the front door and the far room.
Make a paper cone to point the sound down the hallway to the far room.
Agree that whoever hears the bell taps a steel plate near the far room.
challenges.your_turn: Try your idea. One person is the doorbell at the front door. One person is the listener, in the far room. Did the listener hear it? Which idea worked best? Why?

setup.art: A flat seen from above, with a front door at one end and a grown-up in a far bedroom with the door half shut.
setup.caption: 1. The doorbell is at one end. The listener is at the other. How can the sound reach the far room?

setup.art: A girl opening the bedroom door wide while her brother taps a steel tumbler at the front door, sound lines going down the hallway.
setup.caption: 2. Try your idea. Did the listener hear it?

flow.do: Read the problem. One person goes to the far room to be the listener. Tap the tumbler at the front door. Did the listener hear it?
flow.say: You are in the far room. I am the doorbell. Can you hear me? How could we help the sound get to you?
flow.kid: The listener can't hear the bell. How can the sound reach the far room?

ask.q: Why is the bell hard to hear in the far room?
good: It is far away.
The sound spreads out on the way.
The door is half shut.

flow.do: Let your child try two or three ideas. Tap the tumbler the same way each time. The listener says loud, soft or can't hear.
flow.say: Try your idea. I will ring the bell the same way. Could you hear it? Was it loud or soft?
flow.kid: Try your idea. Ask the listener if they heard it.
flow.parent: Help only if asked. Good ideas make the path shorter or more open, or send the sound one way.

flow.do: Ask your child which idea worked best, and why.
flow.say: Which idea helped the listener hear the bell best? Why do you think it worked?
flow.kid: Which idea worked best? Why?

ask.q: Why did opening the door help?
good: The sound did not have to go round the door.
More of the sound could get into the room.

items.p: Say the missing word. The thing that makes a sound is called the sound ____.
items.why: The sound source is the thing that makes the sound, like a bell or a cooker. The sound starts there and travels to your ears.

items.p: Draw a bell in the middle of the page. Draw sound lines going out from the bell. Which ways do they go?
items.a: Sound lines going out on every side of the bell: up, down, left and right.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the sound spreading out to every side, not only one way.
items.art: An empty box with a small bell drawn in the middle.

items.p: In the Walk Away test, which sound faded first, after only a few steps?
opts: Both faded at the same spot
items.why: The finger rub is a very small sound to start with. It spreads out and fades after only a few steps. The tumbler makes a bigger sound, so it travels further.

items.p: Someone claps their hands behind you. You cannot hear the clap, because you are not facing them.
items.why: False. A sound spreads out to every side. You can hear a clap from behind you, as you heard the tumbler from behind in All Around the Tumbler.

items.p: A grown-up reads each sound. Is it near or far? Draw a line to the right box.
items: A friend whispering into my ear
Thunder from a storm over the sea
A clap right next to me
A train horn heard at night from far off
A koel calling from a tree down the road
items.why: Close sounds have travelled only a short way. Far sounds have travelled a long way and spread out, so they often sound soft.
items.art: Two boxes, one with a child's face close up and one with a faraway hill, and six small sound pictures.

items.p: Look at the picture of a flat. The cooker is whistling in the kitchen. A grown-up points to each room. Say 'loud' or 'soft', and the grown-up writes it.
labels: the hall next to the kitchen
the far bedroom with the door shut
items.why: Close to the cooker, the whistle is loud. In the far bedroom it has spread out more, and the shut door also makes it softer.
items.art: A simple map of a flat with a whistling cooker in the kitchen, a hall next to it, and a far bedroom with a closed door.

items.p: Say it out loud, and a grown-up writes it down. In the Walk Away test, why did you stop hearing the finger rub?
items.a: I was too far away. The sound spread out, so not enough of it reached my ears.
items.why: A strong answer says that the sound was still being made, but it was too soft to hear from far away, because it spread out on the way.

items.p: Draw a line from each problem to the best fix.
pairs: I can't hear a whisper from far away
My friend across the road can't hear me
Someone in the far room can't hear the doorbell
Open the doors on the way
items.why: Coming closer means the sound travels less far. A cone sends more of your voice one way. With the doors open, the sound has an open path and does not have to go round them.
items.art: Three small pictures on the left: a girl whispering far away, two girls on balconies, a person in a far room. Three on the right: footsteps, a paper cone, an open door.

items.p: Three of these people will hear the temple bell. One is too far away to hear it. Circle the one who is too far.
opts: Her friend at the temple gate
Her aunt across the temple pond
items.why: The bell's sound spreads out and gets softer as it travels. In another town, it is far too soft to hear. The others are close enough.
items.art: A temple bell, with a girl next to it, a friend at the gate, an aunt across a pond, and a tiny faraway town.

items.p: Kavya wants her grandmother on the balcony to hear her. Three children have ideas.

views.says: Shout as loud as you can.
Use a paper cone and point it at the balcony.
Walk to the balcony and talk in your normal voice.

items.ask: Which idea would you choose? Why? Then say one good thing about another idea.
items.a: Any choice with a good reason. A shout is loud but can hurt your throat and disturb others. A cone sends more of the sound to the balcony without shouting. Walking over is clearest, because the sound has only a short way to travel, but it takes longer.
items.why: A strong answer gives a reason that uses how sound travels, and says fairly what is good about another idea.

items.p: Put the Walk Away test in order. Number them 1, 2 and 3.
items: Put a chappal where the sound faded
Guess which sound will go furthest
Close your eyes and step back each time you hear it
a: Guess which sound will go furthest
Close your eyes and step back each time you hear it
Put a chappal where the sound faded
items.why: First we guess, then we test by stepping back and listening, then we mark where each sound faded.

items.p: The finger rub was too far away to hear, so the sound had stopped.
items.why: False. The fingers were still rubbing, so the sound was still being made. It had spread out so much that too little of it reached your ears.

items.p: Say the missing word. A sound gets ____ the further it travels.
items.why: As a sound travels, it spreads out. So less of it reaches each ear, and it sounds softer.

items.p: Four children stand 1, 3, 6 and 10 steps from a ringing bell. Who hears the bell softest?
items.why: The further away you stand, the more the sound has spread out. So the child 10 steps away hears the least of it.

items.p: Draw yourself calling a friend with a paper cone. Draw the sound lines coming out of the cone.
items.a: A child speaking into the narrow end of a cone, with most sound lines going out of the wide end towards the friend.
items.why: A strong drawing shows most of the sound lines going one way, out of the wide end, towards the friend.

items.p: Say it out loud, and a grown-up writes it down. You stood round the corner of the door and still heard the tumbler. How did the sound get to you?
items.a: The sound spread out to every side. Some of it went through the doorway and spread round the corner to me.
items.why: A strong answer says the sound spreads out on every side, so it can go through the doorway and round the corner.

items.p: Look at the picture of a girl tapping a tumbler. Three children stand near and far. A grown-up points to each child. Say 'loud', 'soft' or 'can't hear', and the grown-up writes it.
labels: the boy far down the road
items.why: The closer you are, the less the sound has spread out, and the louder it is. Far down the road, the sound is too soft to hear.
items.art: A girl tapping a tumbler on a doorstep, a boy right next to her, a girl across the room, and a tiny boy far down the road.

items.p: In the Walk Away test, Meenakshi, a girl in Class 1, heard the finger rub for 3 steps and the crinkly bag for 7 steps. How many more steps did the bag travel?
items.why: Count on from 3 to 7: 4, 5, 6, 7. That is 4 more steps. The bag made a bigger sound, so it travelled further before it faded.

items.p: A cooker whistles in the kitchen. Two friends talk about why it sounds soft in the far bedroom.

views.says: The sound gets tired as it walks far.
The sound spreads out to every room, so less of it reaches the bedroom.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? What did you see in your own tests that helps you decide? Then say what is good about the other idea.
items.a: Zoya's idea matches the tests. The sound spreads out to every side, so less of it reaches far away. Divya is right that far means soft, but sounds do not get tired. With a cone, which stops some of the spreading, a far voice sounds louder.
items.why: A strong answer uses evidence, like the cone test or the finger rub fading, and is fair to Divya: she noticed that far sounds are softer.

items.p: Say it out loud, and a grown-up writes it down. A friend says: 'A sound only goes the way the speaker is facing.' What would you ask your friend to try, to see if that is true?
items.a: Stand behind the person who is making the sound, or round a door, and listen. If you can still hear it, the sound goes every way.
items.why: A strong answer is a test the friend can do, such as listening from behind, and says what they would expect to hear if the sound goes every way.

quiz.p: A bell rings in the next room. How does the sound reach your ears?
opts: Your ears go to the bell
quiz.why: The sound starts at the bell and travels through the air to your ears. Your ears stay where they are and catch it.

quiz.p: What is the sound source when a pressure cooker whistles?
quiz.why: The sound source is the thing that makes the sound. The whistle starts at the cooker, then travels to you.

quiz.p: You can hear the neighbour's mixie through the wall. What does that show?
opts: Sound can travel through a wall
The wall is making the sound
The mixie is in your flat
quiz.why: The mixie is the source, in the neighbour's flat. Its sound travels through the wall to you. Sound can travel through things, as well as through air.

quiz.p: Which sound can you hear from furthest away?
opts: A spoon tapped hard on a steel plate
quiz.why: A hard tap on steel makes a big sound to start with. It can spread out a long way and still be loud enough to hear.

quiz.p: Why is a far-away drum softer than a drum next to you?
opts: Its sound has spread out more on the way
quiz.why: A sound spreads out to every side as it travels. By the time it has come a long way, only a little of it reaches your ears.

quiz.p: A grown-up taps a tumbler in the middle of the room. Where can you hear it?
opts: In front, behind, at the sides and round the door
Only if you can see it
quiz.why: A sound spreads out to every side from its source. In All Around the Tumbler, the tap reached every spot.

quiz.p: What does a paper cone do to your voice?
opts: It sends more of it one way
quiz.why: The cone stops your voice spreading out to the sides. More of it goes out of the wide end, so people in front hear you better.

quiz.p: You see lightning, then hear thunder. Why does the thunder come later?
opts: The sound takes time to travel to you
Thunder is made after the lightning
quiz.why: Lightning and thunder are made at the same moment. The light reaches you almost at once. The sound takes longer to travel.

quiz.p: After a flash, you count to 2 before the thunder. Is the storm near or far?
quiz.why: A short count means the sound did not have far to travel. So the storm is quite near. A long count means it is far.

quiz.p: An ambulance siren is heard from far away. Why?
opts: It is a big sound to start with, so it can spread a long way and still be heard
The siren sends its sound only to your ears
Sound does not get softer when it travels
quiz.why: A loud sound starts big. It spreads out as it travels, but enough of it still reaches ears far away.

videos.title: What causes thunder and lightning (Dr Binocs)
videos.why: Explains thunder and lightning for children, including why we see the flash before we hear the thunder, so they learn that sound takes time to travel.
videos.check: Found by search: "What Causes Thunder & Lightning? | THUNDERSTORM | The Dr Binocs Show | Peekaboo Kidz" by Peekaboo Kidz, 5 minutes 38 seconds. A parent may preview it.

videos.title: Working of a megaphone
videos.why: Shows how a cone sends a voice one way, like the paper cone in the experiment.
videos.check: Found by search: "Working of a megaphone | Sound | Physics" by KClassScienceChannel, 1 minute 44 seconds. A parent may preview it.

videos.title: Ripples on a pond
videos.why: Real footage of ripples spreading out on every side across a pond, a picture of how a sound spreads out from its source. Sound is not a water ripple.
videos.check: Found by search: "Ripples on a pond" by IRIS Earthquake Science, 11 seconds. A parent may preview it.

applications: Ambulances and fire engines use loud sirens, so that the sound travels far ahead and people move out of the way.
Festival loudspeakers are often shaped like cones, so they send the sound one way, towards the crowd.
Lifeguards and police use megaphones to call people far away.
Weather watchers count from lightning to thunder to tell whether a storm is coming closer.
Schools ring one loud bell in the middle of the building, so the sound spreads to every classroom.

spotted.text: In Chennai, vegetable and fish sellers walk down the street calling out what they sell. People hear them from the fourth and fifth floors of a building.
spotted.art: A woman pushing a vegetable cart down a street in Chennai, calling out, and a girl leaning out of a high balcony to listen.

spotted.text: During the Kerala monsoon in June, families see the lightning over the sea first and hear the thunder a few moments later.
spotted.art: A white lightning flash over a dark sea near a Kerala beach, with coconut trees and a family watching from a window.

spotted.text: At Ganesh Chaturthi in Mumbai and Pune, cone-shaped loudspeakers on poles send music and announcements along the street.
spotted.art: A street decorated for Ganesh Chaturthi, with cone-shaped loudspeakers on a tall pole pointing down the road.

spotted.text: During Durga Puja in Kolkata, people blow the conch shell, and the sound carries across the whole neighbourhood.
spotted.art: A woman in a red-and-white sari blowing a conch shell in front of a lit pandal.

spotted.text: At night, in towns and villages all over India, people hear a train horn from a station far away.
spotted.art: A small town at night, quiet houses, and a train with its light on, far away across the fields.

open_questions.q: Why does a sound sometimes carry much further on a cool, still night than on a hot afternoon?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know that wind and warm and cool layers of air bend a sound up or down as it travels. Working out exactly how far a sound will carry on a given day is still hard, and people are still studying it.

open_questions.q: How do our ears and brain tell which way a sound came from?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know that having two ears helps, because a sound reaches one ear a tiny moment before the other. Some parts of how the brain works this out, especially for sounds from above or behind, are still being studied.

open_questions.q: Why do some places carry sound much better than others?
open_questions.why_open: The shape of a building, the walls and even the air temperature change how a sound travels. Builders and scientists still test old forts, temples and halls to understand why some carry sound so well.

ask_kids: What is the furthest-away sound you can hear right now?
Can you hear the cooker from your bedroom? Why do you think so?
If you whisper to me from the next room, will I hear you? Let's try.
Which way does your voice go when you talk: only forward, or every way?
When you see lightning tonight, shall we count to the thunder?
What sound from outside reaches our home every morning? Where does it start?

maths.problem: In the Walk Away test, Lakshmi heard the finger rub for 3 steps, the crinkly bag for 6 steps, and the tumbler for 10 steps. Put the sounds in order, from the one that travelled least far to the one that travelled furthest.
maths.answer: The finger rub (3 steps), then the bag (6 steps), then the tumbler (10 steps).
maths.explain: 3 is less than 6, and 6 is less than 10. So the finger rub went least far and the tumbler went furthest.
maths.context: This is about the Walk Away test, where you stepped back until each sound faded.
maths.why_maths: Putting the numbers in order shows at a glance which sound travelled furthest.

maths.problem: Nila counted to 6 after the first lightning flash and to 3 after the second. Was the storm closer the first time or the second time? How many fewer did she count the second time?
maths.answer: Closer the second time. She counted 3 fewer.
maths.explain: A shorter count means the thunder had less far to travel, so the storm was closer. Count down from 6 to 3: 5, 4, 3. That is 3 fewer.
maths.context: This is about counting from the lightning to the thunder.
maths.why_maths: Comparing two counts tells you whether the storm is coming closer or going away.

maths.problem: Zoya can hear the whisper from 2 steps away. Her brother is 5 steps away. How many steps must he walk to hear it?
maths.explain: He is at 5. He needs to get to 2. Count down from 5: 4, 3, 2. That is 3 steps.
maths.context: This is about Whisper Walk, where walkers step closer until they hear the word.
maths.why_maths: Working out the difference tells you how much closer you must come before a soft sound reaches you.

maths.problem: Look at your cooker map. Count the rooms you coloured red, yellow and blue. Which colour has the most rooms?
maths.answer: It depends on your home. For example: red 2 rooms, yellow 2 rooms, blue 1 room. Red and yellow are equal, and blue has the fewest.
maths.explain: Count each colour and write the number. Then compare the numbers. The biggest number has the most rooms.
maths.context: This is about the cooker map, where you coloured each room by how loud the whistle was.
maths.why_maths: Counting each group shows whether the whistle reaches most of your home or only a few rooms.

warmup.a: Yes. A sound spreads out to every side.

roots.context: We have walked away from sounds, listened from behind a door and called through a paper cone. Now we ask what a travelling sound tells us about the world, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: In All Around the Tumbler, one tap reached you in front, behind and round the door. The sound spread out to fill the whole room at once. Far away, it had spread over more space, so less of it reached you. So one sound is shared out among every place around it.
deep_truth.habit: We picture a sound going from one thing to one ear, like a ball thrown to a catcher. But a sound spreads out to every side, and every ear around it catches a share of the same sound.
deep_truth.evidence: In All Around the Tumbler, the same tap reached every spot in the room and round the door. In the Walk Away test, the same finger rub was clear close by and gone a few steps back, where its share had become too small to hear.

three.who_am_i: You are a listener in one spot. Every sound you hear has travelled to that spot, from somewhere else, to reach you.
three.what_is_life: Many living beings send sounds across distances to stay together: a calf calling her mother, crows calling across the city, people calling each other home.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is full of sounds spreading out from many places at once, crossing each other in the air, reaching everyone a little differently.

roots.thread: One bell rings in one place. Its sound spreads out on every side and reaches everyone around it: a child near the bell, a grandmother across the pond, a crow on the roof. One sound becomes a different sound in each ear, louder or softer. The air that carries it is aware in its own way, and so are the bell and every listener. Many scientists disagree: they say only beings with nerves are aware.

teachings.source: The Nyaya philosophers of India, as summed up by Vishvanatha in the Bhasha-pariccheda (17th century), in the verses on sound
teachings.teaching: A sound makes the next sound next to it, and that one makes the next, until a sound reaches the ear. It spreads like ripples on a pond, one ring after another. Some teachers said it spreads like a kadamba flower, whose buds open on every side at once.
teachings.link: In All Around the Tumbler, the tap reached you in front, behind and at the sides. In Be the Air, the tap was passed from person to person. These old thinkers described the same spreading and passing on, by thinking about ripples and flowers.

teachings.source: The Udana 6.4, a Buddhist text, which tells the story of the blind men and the elephant (Jain teachers tell this story too)
teachings.teaching: Several blind men each touched one part of an elephant. One felt the trunk, one the ear, one the leg. Each one described a different elephant, and each was right about the part he touched.
teachings.link: In Who Hears It Louder?, Meena by the bell heard a loud sound, and her friend at the end of the street heard a soft one. It was one bell. Each of them told the truth about what reached their own ears.

science.text: A sound spreads out to every side from its source. The further it travels, the more it has spread out, so it sounds softer.
Sound takes time to travel through air: about three seconds to go one kilometre.

other_view.view: They say air, bells and tumblers are not aware of anything. To them, sound is only air pushing on air. They think awareness belongs to living beings with nerves or brains.

practice.title: The furthest sound
practice.say: Sit comfortably and close your eyes. First, listen to the closest sound you can hear. Maybe your own breathing. Now listen a little further, to a sound in this room. Now further, to a sound outside the room. Now as far as you can. What is the furthest sound you can hear? Every one of those sounds has travelled all the way to you.
practice.kid: Close your eyes. Hear the closest sound. Now a sound further away. Now the furthest sound you can. It travelled all the way to you.

ask: When the finger rub was too far away for you, could someone closer still hear it? Was the sound loud or soft, then?
One bell, many listeners, each hearing it a little differently. Which one hears the real sound?
Where does a sound go after it has passed you?
roots.art: A temple bell ringing in the middle, with rings of sound spreading out to a child close by, a grown-up across a pond, a crow on a roof and a dog far down a lane, each ring a little fainter.

how_we_found_out.story: For a very long time, people knew that thunder comes after lightning. But many thought a sound reaches us the moment it is made. Writers in the school of the Greek thinker Aristotle also taught that high, sharp sounds travel faster than deep ones. In the 1630s, two French scientists, Marin Mersenne and Pierre Gassendi, tested these ideas. They stood far away from someone firing a gun. They saw the flash and smoke at once. The bang came later. They timed the wait. The further away they stood, the longer the wait. So a sound takes time to travel. Gassendi also compared a big gun, with a deep boom, and a small gun, with a sharp crack. From far away, both bangs arrived after the same wait. So high and deep sounds travel at the same speed. That old teaching was wrong. You can test the same idea in any monsoon storm: count from the flash to the thunder.
how_we_found_out.who: Marin Mersenne (1588 to 1648) and Pierre Gassendi (1592 to 1655), French scientists
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Writers in Aristotle's school taught that high sounds travel faster than deep sounds. Gassendi timed a deep boom and a sharp crack from far away, and both arrived after the same wait.

founder: ideas/by_topic/sound.md, 'How sound travels' and 'Sound waves': the paper cone megaphone became the Paper Cone experiment. The human wave relay and passing a shoulder squeeze became Be the Air. Hearing through a closed door versus an open one became the cooker map and the round-the-door listening. The whisper relay became Whisper Walk. Distant thunder became Count After the Lightning. The string telephone, knocking on materials, echo timing and the vacuum jar belong to the Level 4 and Level 5 units, so this unit does not use them.

Curriculum entry sci.sound.sound-moves.L1 (Sounds move from the source to our ears), Cambridge Stage 1 unit 6.3 'Sounds move': how far loud and quiet sounds go (Activity 6.3) and the megaphone. The Level 1 unit sci.sound.sources-of-sound.L1 teaches sound sources and loud and soft, and this unit leads on from it. The Level 3 unit sci.sound.sources-of-sound.L3 uses the coin line for air passing on a sound, and the hearing unit uses ear covers and pitch tests, so this unit does not repeat them.
science: Inverse-square spreading: sound intensity from a small source in open air falls with the square of distance (about 6 decibels per doubling of distance). Indoors, reflections from walls make the fall-off slower.
Speed of sound in air at about 20 degrees Celsius: about 343 metres per second, so about 3 seconds per kilometre.

Marin Mersenne, Harmonie universelle (1636), gave a speed of sound from gun-flash timing. Pierre Gassendi's timings (1630s) found loud and soft, high and low gun sounds travelled at the same speed, against Aristotle's view that high notes travel faster.
Horn and cone megaphones increase forward sound by directing it and matching the voice to the air better; the gain is modest for a paper cone but audible.

Nyaya-Vaisheshika on sound propagation: vichi-taranga-nyaya (the maxim of waves and ripples) and kadamba-mukula-nyaya (the maxim of kadamba buds), Vishvanatha's Bhasha-pariccheda (Karikavali). Verse numbers not checked.
Udana 6.4 (Tittha Sutta), the parable of the blind men and the elephant.

playtest: Walked through every experiment, activity, game and project as a family in a flat, and checked minutes, steps and checks against each other. Whisper Walk had 12 cards but only 10 minutes, so it is now 6 written-out cards, the whisperer changes after every card (works for 2 and 4 players), and ties are shared wins. Who Hears It Louder also says what happens on a tie. The three video entries still have no checked address (the validator needs three), so they stay to be found.
